To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

poverty levels and percentages of blacks and Hispanics are negatively associated with spatial access to parks, green spaces, and open spaces in urban/suburbia, while they are positively linked in rural areas.

poverty levels were negatively associated (inversely related) with distances to parks in urban and suburban areas while positively associated (directly related) in rural areas, and percentages of blacks and Hispanics in general were negatively linked to distances and green space coverage across the urbanization continuum.

poverty levels and percentages of blacks and Hispanics in the conterminuous USA are negatively associated with distances and green space coverage to parks, and these associations are different across urban, suburban, and rural areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the spatial distributions of parks and greenspaces are related to the spatial distribution of racial/ethnic minorities and poverty in the USA.
how the spatial distribution of parks and green space varies across the urban–suburban–rural continuum, and how this spatial distribution varies by race–ethnicity, poverty status, and age groups.
the distribution of park and green spaces across the urbanization spectrum in the USA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
spatial access to parks is a social justice issue, and the associations are context dependent.
the spatial disparities in access to green spaces and parks are not uniform across the urban–suburban–rural continuum.
there are disparities in the spatial distribution of parks and green space across the urbanization spectrum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spatial disparities in the distribution of parks and green space are more pronounced in rural areas than in urban/suburban regions.
there is a need to address the spatial inequity in the distributions of parks and open spaces in the USA.
the urban–rurban continuum matters in terms of the relationship between race, ethnicity and poverty with access to parks and greenspaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of parks and green space in the USA is not equitable, and the spatial disparities are more pronounced in urban areas.
the urban–rurban continuum should be considered when examining the spatial disparities in the distribution of parks and green space.
the urban–rURAL continuum is an important contextual variable that should be taken into account when examining spatial disparities in the distribution of parks and green space in the USA.
